11 Some small solid cubes each have mass 1.0 kg and sides of length 5.0 cm. These small cubes
are stacked together to form a large solid cube with sides of length 2.0 m.
What is the weight of the large cube?
A
0.39 kN
B
0.39 MN
C
0.63 MN
D
0.63 GN

hints: Convert $5.0 \text{ cm}$ to metres and find how many small $0.050 \text{ m}$ lengths fit along one $2.0 \text{ m}$ edge of the large cube.
The large cube is filled in three dimensions, so the total number of $1.0 \text{ kg}$ cubes is the per-edge number cubed, not the per-edge number itself.
Multiply the total number by $1.0 \text{ kg}$ to get total mass, then use $W = mg$ with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and check whether the result is in $\text{kN}$, $\text{MN}$ or $\text{GN}$.
walkthrough: Convert the small side to metres: $5.0 \text{ cm} = 0.050 \text{ m}$. Number along one edge is $N = 2.0/0.050 = 40$.
Because volume fills in length, width and height, total number of small cubes is $N^3 = 40^3 = 64000$.
Each small cube has mass $1.0 \text{ kg}$, so total mass is $M = 64000 \times 1.0 = 64000 \text{ kg}$.
Weight is $W = Mg$. Substituting gives $W = 64000 \times 9.81 = 627840 \text{ N}$.
Convert to meganewtons: $627840 \text{ N} \approx 0.63 \times 10^6 \text{ N} = 0.63 \text{ MN}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: This uses only the linear ratio $2.0/0.05 = 40$ cubes, giving about $390 \text{ N}$, instead of cubing the ratio to fill the volume.

B.explanation: This is $1000$ times too large for the linear-ratio mass of $40 \text{ kg}$, caused by confusing $\text{kN}$ with $\text{MN}$.

C.explanation: The $40^3 = 64000$ small cubes give mass $64000 \text{ kg}$ and weight $mg \approx 0.63 \text{ MN}$.

D.explanation: This has the correct digits for $64000 \times g$ but is $1000$ times too large by using $\text{GN}$ instead of $\text{MN}$.
